title: How Swearing at Work Works
summary: Editor Candice Gibson and staff writer Josh Clark discuss whether swearing at work is a good thing, based on a University of East Anglia study of a British mail order warehouse that found swearing built social bonds among employees, while executives swore less. They discuss the FCC's rules on fleeting expletives and indecency, the Parents Television Council's complaints about Gossip Girl and 30 Rock, and the PTC's count of profanity on television during the family hour (815 foul words in 180 hours, about 4.53 per hour). The episode opens and closes with ad reads for a camera.

segments.title: Opening camera ad read
segments.summary: Opening sponsor read for a camera, repeated at the end of the episode.

segments.title: Introduction and swearing at work campaign
segments.summary: Candice and Josh introduce the topic of whether swearing at work is good, with Josh joking about a swear-at-work campaign after his Hawaiian shirt campaign fell flat.

segments.title: University of East Anglia study on workplace swearing
segments.summary: The hosts describe a British study at the University of East Anglia in a mail order warehouse. Swearing among workers built relationships and trust, while executives swore much less. The study authors hoped HR directors would tolerate swearing.

segments.title: FCC rules and the Parents Television Council
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the FCC's treatment of fleeting expletives and sexual or bathroom content, and the Parents Television Council's campaigns against Gossip Girl and an episode of 30 Rock.

segments.title: Counting profanity on television
segments.summary: The PTC's studies of profanity during the family hour (8 to 9 pm) found 815 foul words in 180 hours of programming, about 4.53 swears per hour, showing an increase from 2001 to 2006.

segments.title: Sign-off and closing ad
segments.summary: Josh is directed to his article on swearing at work, the hosts sign off, and the camera ad plays again.
